question: How do chemical data, molecular and reaction representations, machine-learning models, language models, and autonomous laboratories fit into a common AI-for-chemistry workflow?

key_findings.claim: The survey organizes AI chemistry as a pipeline from data acquisition through representation and modeling to property prediction, generation, retrosynthesis, and autonomous experimentation.
key_findings.evidence: Separate sections cover molecular and reaction data, identifiers and learned representations, predictive and generative applications, reaction planning, robotic laboratories, and chemical LLMs.

key_findings.claim: Chemical datasets remain fragmented and biased even though widely used resources span molecules, quantum trajectories, toxicity, reactions, and high-throughput experiments.
key_findings.evidence: The paper catalogs ZINC, MD17, QM7/8/9, Tox21, MoleculeNet, USPTO derivatives, and HTE sources, while emphasizing lab silos, inconsistent conditions, scarce negative results, and instrument-dependent variation.

key_findings.claim: Hand-engineered representations offer chemical grounding, while learned graph, transformer, contrastive, and 3D representations offer flexibility but often lack explicit chemical interpretability.
key_findings.evidence: The comparison spans SMILES, InChI, SELFIES, fingerprints and descriptors versus GNN and language-model embeddings, and proposes hybrids that combine learned features with chemistry-informed structure.

key_findings.claim: AI methods now cover property prediction, de novo design, and single- and multi-step retrosynthesis, but each application inherits validity and evaluation risks from representations and data.
key_findings.evidence: The application review contrasts VAEs, GANs, diffusion and reinforcement learning for generation and template-based versus template-free reaction prediction and search for synthesis planning.

key_findings.claim: The most ambitious systems close the loop between inference and experiments through robotics, spectroscopy, simulation, and adaptive exploration.
key_findings.evidence: The survey describes autonomous-laboratory stacks and AI-EDISON, which combines spectroscopy, simulation, and open-ended or quality-diversity exploration and reports yields up to 95% in its demonstrations.

key_findings.claim: Chemical LLMs and agents are promising interfaces but next-token fluency does not guarantee molecular or reaction validity.
key_findings.evidence: The taxonomy includes ChemCrow, Coscientist, ChatMOF, RXNFP and ChemLLM, while warning about format conversion, hallucinated atoms or functional groups, chemically unreasonable molecules, and objectives not tailored to chemical knowledge.

key_findings.claim: The review is broad but cannot establish comparative effectiveness because it lacks a systematic search protocol, quantitative meta-analysis, and prospective head-to-head validation.
key_findings.evidence: The article narratively selects datasets, systems, and examples without reported database queries, inclusion criteria, study-quality scoring, or normalized performance aggregation.

method.core_idea: Provide an end-to-end taxonomy of AI in chemistry centered on the dependency chain from chemical evidence and representation to models, applications, and automated discovery loops.
method.mechanism: The survey groups prior work by data type, molecular or reaction encoding, learning paradigm, downstream task, and degree of experimental autonomy, then identifies cross-cutting bottlenecks in data quality, interpretability, and domain validity.
assumptions: The selected literature adequately represents the fast-moving field despite no systematic inclusion protocol.
Tasks with different chemical endpoints can be compared within a common pipeline taxonomy.
Reported benchmark improvements translate into useful wet-lab decisions.
Autonomous-agent reliability can improve through domain models, tools, and standardized data.

techniques.role: Maps data, representation, model, application, and laboratory feedback into one workflow.
Contrasts symbolic strings, fingerprints, graphs, 3D geometry, and learned embeddings.
Separates prediction, generation, retrosynthesis, and experiment automation.
Distinguishes agents, domain models, downstream encoders, and evaluation benchmarks.

evaluations.setting: Narrative synthesis of molecular, quantum, toxicity, reaction, and HTE datasets.
evaluations.metric: Coverage of data type, scale, annotation, and known quality constraints.
evaluations.result: The catalog exposes broad resource availability alongside scarcity, heterogeneity, and reporting bias.
evaluations.baseline: No formal baseline; this is a survey taxonomy.

evaluations.setting: Cross-application review of property prediction, generation, and retrosynthesis.
evaluations.metric: Representative model classes, benchmark practices, and deployment constraints.
evaluations.result: No single model family dominates the pipeline; representation and data validity constrain every task.
evaluations.baseline: Traditional descriptors, rule/template systems, and physics-based simulation where discussed.

evaluations.setting: Autonomous chemistry systems and chemical LLM agents.
evaluations.metric: Degree of closed-loop operation and reported experimental outcomes.
evaluations.result: Tool-using agents and robotic loops demonstrate integrated workflows, but the survey supplies no normalized reliability or cost comparison.

limitations: No systematic-search, inclusion, or study-quality protocol is reported.
Results from heterogeneous chemical tasks are not normalized into a quantitative meta-analysis.
Many claims depend on benchmark or demonstration results rather than prospective multi-lab replication.
The rapidly changing LLM and autonomous-lab sections can become outdated quickly.
Environmental, safety, synthesis-cost, and uncertainty metrics receive less consistent treatment than task accuracy or yield.
failure_modes: Dataset leakage or scaffold overlap can make molecular benchmarks overstate generalization.
A syntactically valid SMILES string can still describe an unstable, toxic, unavailable, or unsynthesizable molecule.
Reaction data missing failed experiments can bias yield and retrosynthesis models toward reported successes.
Tool-using agents may propagate a hallucinated intermediate into unsafe physical actions.
Performance can collapse across instruments, laboratories, chemical regimes, or representation conversions.
reusable_insights: Evaluate chemical AI as an evidence pipeline rather than an isolated prediction metric.
Combine domain-grounded descriptors with learned representations when interpretability and extrapolation both matter.
Preserve negative experiments and complete conditions as first-class training data.
Require structure, reaction, safety, and wet-lab validation at increasingly consequential stages of an autonomous loop.
open_questions: Which standardized splits best measure extrapolation to new scaffolds, reactions, and laboratories?
How should uncertainty and chemical constraint violations gate autonomous-agent actions?
Can reporting standards make negative and failed experiments reusable across institutions?
What prospective benchmark jointly measures discovery value, synthesis success, cost, safety, and time?

competitive_landscape.title: A Review of Large Language Models and Autonomous Agents in Chemistry
competitive_landscape.relationship: Focused survey of the chemical-LLM and agent portion of the field.
competitive_landscape.difference: That review gives greater depth to LLM architectures and autonomous agents; this paper embeds those systems in a broader data-to-laboratory chemistry pipeline.

competitive_landscape.title: From Generalist to Specialist: A Survey of Large Language Models for Chemistry
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary specialist survey of chemistry-oriented language models.
competitive_landscape.difference: The specialist survey systematizes model adaptation and chemical capabilities; this review devotes more coverage to datasets, conventional ML, retrosynthesis, and robotic laboratories.

competitive_landscape.title: Machine Learning in Chemistry: Data and Algorithms
competitive_landscape.relationship: Established review of the data representations and algorithms underlying chemical machine learning.
competitive_landscape.difference: The Nature review centers foundational data and algorithm choices before the current agent wave; this paper expands the scope to modern generative models, LLM agents, and autonomous closed loops.

competitive_landscape.title: Recent Advances in Artificial Intelligence for Retrosynthesis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Task-specific review of a major application covered by the paper.
competitive_landscape.difference: The retrosynthesis survey provides deeper coverage of single- and multi-step planning and evaluation; this paper trades depth for an end-to-end map linking planning to representations and automation.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a comprehensive overview connecting foundational chemical data and representations to AI models, core applications, language agents, and autonomous discovery.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Its value is broad integration and accessibility rather than a novel algorithm or definitive evidence synthesis. Multiple narrower reviews cover individual segments more deeply; the differentiator is the single end-to-end workflow, limited by non-systematic selection and fast obsolescence.

reviewer_notes: Read the full 34-page extraction across data, representations, applications, autonomous systems, LLMs, challenges, and conclusion. Competitor records were checked using primary arXiv and RSC publisher pages on 2026-08-23.
